The story we keep telling This is where invention enters. The psychologist Dan McAdams argues that from late adolescence we build a narra- tive identity, weaving past, present and imagined future into a story with turning points, setbacks and meaning. Two people with identical biographies can become different selves depending on how they tell them. McAdams and others have found that people who re- count hardship as a path toward growth, rather than a permanent injury, tend to report greater well-being. Reinvention can be dramatic. In 1848 a railway foreman named Phineas Gage survived an iron rod passing through his skull. Popular accounts claim he became a different man, coarse and unreliable. Later scholarship suggests the legend was inflated and that Gage eventually rebuilt a working life, driving stage- coaches in Chile. Whatever the injury took, he found a way to author a new chapter. Presence is a form of attention The psychologist Elaine Hatfield spent decades studying emotional con- tagion, the way moods pass between people through tiny, unconscious mim- icry of faces, voices and posture. An anxious person unsettles a meeting be- fore anyone names the anxiety. A calm one does the reverse. The room borrows their weather. This may be the most useful clue about the magnetic ones. Many of them are not performing at all. They are lis- tening. The philosopher Simone Weil called attention the rarest and purest form of generosity and anyone who has been fully attended to knows why. When someone puts down their phone, stops composing their next sentence and simply takes you in, you feel larger in their company. Perhaps that is the glow we have al- ways tried to describe. It is not light emitted by them. It is the warmth of being truly seen and it is felt by the one who receives it.
What older traditions noticed Contemplative traditions spent cen- turies training this quality. In Hindu practice, darshan means the exchange of sight between devotee and holy figure, a meeting in which looking is itself a gift. Buddhist teachers cultivate equanimity until it becomes visible in the face. Quaker meetings sit in silence and trust that a settled person settles others.
